classification.tone: Darkly comic, feverish, surreal, and increasingly nightmarish

evaluation.positioning_hook: A frustrated Flagstaff accountant makes a drunken wish for a better life, then wakes inside the movie-star fantasy he’s been craving — with his family now belonging to someone else.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise has a clean commercial engine: midlife dissatisfaction, a supernatural bargain, and a family-home showdown that escalates into horror. The movie-star fantasy gives it a broad hook, though the tonal swing into surreal identity horror keeps it a little more specialized than a four-quadrant thriller.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The script announces its engine early with the nightmare opening, the December 20th date, and the bar encounter with Gene. By the time Champ wakes in the blood-soaked bedroom and later discovers the set/reality split, the premise is unmistakable.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Champ is a strong lead because his hunger, shame, and vanity are all dramatized in action, not just dialogue. Gene is an excellent counterforce, and Cheyenne has real emotional gravity, though the supporting players mostly orbit the central duel.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a big swing by turning a midlife crisis into a supernatural identity swap wrapped inside a movie production. The meta reveal at the end and the recurring green-eye motif give the piece a confident, memorable signature.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps generating new turns — the bar pact, the mansion fantasy, the production-set reveal, the journal discovery, the premiere confrontation, and the final blizzard showdown. A few stretches lean on repetition of the same emotional argument, but the escalation stays active and readable.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The core idea feels fresh because it fuses a very human regret fantasy with a supernatural body-swap morality tale and a movie-set meta layer. The ending lands as something both strange and inevitable once the rules are clear.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Flagstaff is rendered with specific texture — snow, diners, an arthouse theater, office life, and the local theater-kid past — and the Hollywood/production world adds another layer. The setting is more than backdrop, though the story’s main energy still comes from the central premise rather than a deeply networked ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a distinct tonal fingerprint: suburban dread, absurd celebrity fantasy, deadpan office humiliation, and escalating supernatural horror all coexist in the same frame. The humming motif, the green-eyed menace, and the self-aware production world make the tone easy to identify.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the genre machinery, the script is really about regret, masculinity, marriage, and the seduction of being seen. The final turn toward self-acceptance gives the piece emotional aftertaste, even though the surface engine is the main attraction.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Champ/Cheyenne/Gene is a strong triangle with real friction, and Gerry adds a useful emotional pressure point. Beyond that, the office and production characters function well but are mostly there to service Champ’s arc rather than create a broader ensemble web.

casting_characteristics: One male lead in his late 40s/early 50s
Several roles require strong physical resemblance or mirrored casting across the fantasy/reality split

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with substantial exterior snow scenes

technical.vfx_details: Dream-state transitions, blood effects, eye-glow/green-hue moments, body-state shifts, and a few stylized reality/fantasy blends.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood, knife wounds, broken glass, snow effects, and a few impact/fall beats.

rights_flags.detail: Sunset Boulevard is referenced as a film title and screening marquee; It’s a Wonderful Life is shown on TV.
In-N-Out, Range Rover, Rolls Royce, VW Beetle, and Lego are all named on the page.
Sunset Boulevard and It’s a Wonderful Life are plot-visible screen references that may require clearance depending on use.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Premium streaming or theatrical genre lane
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with festival-to-platform or specialty theatrical potential

cost.note: Contained character drama with a modest location footprint, but the snow work, LA intercuts, mansion, premiere sequence, and stylized effects push it above micro-budget.

cast.note: The script depends on three strong adult leads, two child roles, and mirrored casting across the movie-set/family-reality split.

location.note: The story moves between Flagstaff homes, office space, an arthouse theater, a diner, Hollywood Boulevard, a mansion, and a premiere venue.

content.note: Knife violence, blood, psychological distress, and a murder fantasy keep it firmly in mature territory without pushing into extreme explicitness.

rights.note: Several named brands and recognizable film titles appear on the page, creating a manageable but real clearance pass.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The premise turns midlife envy into horror.
strengths.what_it_means: That gives the project a clean commercial engine: a universal adult fantasy becomes a supernatural nightmare with stakes that are emotional, not abstract. Buyers who want elevated genre with a human wound at the center — and actors who want a role that can play shame, vanity, and terror in one arc — will immediately understand the appeal.
strengths.evidence: Champ’s drunken confession to Gene, the wish for a do-over, and the later reveal that he has traded lives with the man who replaced him.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Champ is a showcase lead role.
strengths.what_it_means: The part gives an actor a full-spectrum performance lane: wounded dad, self-mythologizing dreamer, panicked suspect, and finally a man forced to confront what he actually chose. Prestige-minded performers and mid-career leads looking for a career-reframing role would circle this fast.
strengths.evidence: Champ’s oscillation between comic self-pity, emotional collapse, and violent conviction across the office, bar, set, and home sequences.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Gene is a magnetic antagonist with depth.
strengths.what_it_means: He isn’t just a villain; he’s the dark mirror version of the same hunger, which makes the central conflict feel personal and actor-driven rather than plot-driven. Character actors who can play charm with menace, and buyers who like a duel of equals, will see immediate value.
strengths.evidence: Gene’s calm bar seduction, his family-man disguise, the journal reveal, and his repeated insistence that he understands Champ’s choice.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The movie-set reveal adds a sharp meta layer.
strengths.what_it_means: That twist opens the material beyond a standard possession or body-swap story and gives the ending a self-aware, industry-savvy sting. Directors and buyers who respond to elevated genre with a formal conceit will see a hook that can travel in conversation and marketing.
strengths.evidence: The final act reveal that Champ is on a film set, with Director Mikey, Trish, fake blood, and the production of 12/20.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Flagstaff is used as a story engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The snowy, modest town gives the film a specific visual identity and a built-in contrast against the Hollywood fantasy, which helps the movie feel both intimate and cinematic. Producers looking for a contained but distinctive setting — and audiences who like their genre grounded in a real place — will respond to that specificity.
strengths.evidence: The snowbound house, the arthouse theater, the diner, the office, and the repeated bike-in-snow imagery.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The family triangle has real emotional charge.
strengths.what_it_means: Champ, Cheyenne, and Gene create a triangle that can carry the whole movie because each side wants something legible and contradictory at once. That’s the kind of relationship web that attracts actors, gives a director performance-forward material, and keeps the audience invested even when the story gets surreal.
strengths.evidence: Cheyenne’s shifting recognition, Gene’s protective posture, and Champ’s desperate attempts to be seen as husband and father.

strengths.what_it_means: It blends domestic dread, deadpan comedy, and fever-dream horror in a way that feels specific rather than generic, which is a real moat in the genre marketplace. Buyers chasing elevated, conversation-starting genre pieces and directors with a taste for tonal control will see a clear lane.
strengths.evidence: The humming motif, the office humiliation, the surreal LA fantasy, and the blood-soaked nightmare sequences all coexist without losing the script’s identity.

whats_special.headline: CHAMP has a sharp, marketable engine: a middle-aged man’s wish for a better life becomes a supernatural theft of identity, marriage, and fatherhood. The script’s biggest asset is that it plays like a prestige performance piece inside an elevated genre hook, with a lead role and antagonist that both feel castable, promotable, and memorable.

lead_characters.name: Champney Granger / Champ
lead_characters.hook: A dissatisfied Flagstaff accountant with a theater-kid past, a bruised ego, and a desperate need to matter. He is funny, needy, vain, tender, and increasingly unmoored, which makes him feel like a real man whose private humiliation has finally found a supernatural outlet.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Matthew McConaughey in True Detective season 1 — a charismatic, self-mythologizing man whose interior collapse is the performance. It gives an actor the chance to play comic vanity, marital shame, panic, and moral horror in one escalating arc.

lead_characters.name: Gene Alterno
lead_characters.hook: A fire-breathing street performer who becomes the polished suburban double of Champ’s life, carrying the same hunger but with a colder discipline. He reads as charming, wounded, and predatory all at once, which makes him feel like the version of success that has already paid its price.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Michael Shannon in Take Shelter — a man whose stillness and buried volatility keep the audience leaning in. It gives a character actor the chance to play seduction, menace, remorse, and fatherly authority without ever losing the threat underneath.

lead_characters.name: Cheyenne Granger
lead_characters.hook: Champ’s wife, a painter and emotional anchor who sees more than she says and keeps the family’s center of gravity intact. She has warmth, skepticism, and a quiet steel that makes her more than a spouse in the story — she is the person the fantasy is really trying to win back.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Toni Collette in Hereditary — a woman whose domestic presence gradually reveals enormous emotional force. It gives an actress the chance to play intimacy, suspicion, hurt, and hard-earned clarity in a role that can anchor the film’s heart.

lead_characters.name: Gerry Granger
lead_characters.hook: Champ and Cheyenne’s insecure son, old enough to notice the fractures and young enough to still want his dad to be the hero. He’s prickly, observant, and emotionally exposed, which makes him a pressure point in every family scene.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of emotionally loaded child role that gave Jacob Tremblay in Room such immediate impact — a kid whose reactions carry real dramatic weight. Young actors and parents looking for a meaningful, not decorative, child part will see the value immediately.

lead_characters.name: Becky Granger
lead_characters.hook: The older sibling who moves through the house with teenage independence and a sharper read on the adults than she lets on. She has enough attitude to feel lived-in, and enough vulnerability to make the family dynamic feel complete.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Saoirse Ronan in Lady Bird — a teen who can be funny, cutting, and emotionally legible in the same breath. It gives a young actress a role with attitude and subtext, not just exposition.

lead_characters.name: Trish
lead_characters.hook: Champ’s assistant and the practical voice around the production machine, she keeps the fantasy moving while quietly registering how far off the rails he is. She has a dry, professional energy that makes her feel like the only adult in the room when the movie starts to warp.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of sharp, scene-stealing support role that Allison Janney often turns into a pressure valve — efficient, funny, and emotionally legible in a few scenes. Character actors who can land authority and irony will want it.

lead_characters.name: Director Mikey
lead_characters.hook: The director inside the film-within-the-film, he treats Champ like both a star and a problem child. He gives the meta layer its authority and keeps the production world feeling real rather than gimmicky.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Paul Dano in a supporting authority role — a creative professional whose calm surface hides real control. Directors-turned-actors or actors who can play competence with unease will be drawn to it.

lead_characters.name: Todd
lead_characters.hook: Champ’s boss, who delivers the office disappointment that helps trigger the whole spiral. He’s blunt, ordinary, and oblivious in a way that makes the humiliation feel painfully real.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of grounded authority role that J.K. Simmons has turned into a memorable pressure point in dramas — a man whose plainspoken delivery can change the temperature of a scene. Veteran character actors will know exactly how to make it land.

lead_characters.name: Dan Huntington
lead_characters.hook: The office rival who gets the promotion Champ thinks is his, and who embodies the petty social victory Champ cannot tolerate. He’s smug enough to be irritating, but ordinary enough to feel like the kind of man life rewards by accident.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of office-antagonist role that Stephen Root has made memorable — a small but potent part that can tilt a whole room. Character actors who excel at passive-aggressive comedy with a sting will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Tina
lead_characters.hook: The receptionist who sees Champ as a dreamer before she sees him as a man, which gives the office scenes their flirtation and sting. She’s light, observant, and socially fluent, making her a useful mirror for Champ’s self-image.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of breezy, scene-lifting role that Zooey Deschanel made a calling card in early indie work — a woman who can shift a scene with a smile and a line. Actors who can play charm without losing intelligence will want it.

lead_characters.name: Sandy
lead_characters.hook: The arthouse theater attendant with an uncanny, hard-to-place presence who feels like they know more than they should. Sandy gives the film a slightly mythic gatekeeper energy right before the fantasy fully opens.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of eerie, memorable cameo that Tilda Swinton has turned into an event in smaller roles — a character who can feel like a portal. Actors with a taste for strange, precise supporting work will be interested.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to make a prestige genre film about male regret, identity theft, and the terror of getting what you asked for.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Established indie directors with at least one or two features, or elevated-genre filmmakers moving up from festival horror/thriller work. The material rewards someone who cares about performance first, can hold a surreal premise in a grounded emotional frame, and knows how to make a contained world feel cinematic.
director_appeal.detail: The script gives a director a strong tonal balancing act: domestic realism, meta movie-world satire, and supernatural dread all need to coexist without collapsing into parody. It’s especially attractive to filmmakers who like actor-forward material and can stage a final-act confrontation that feels both intimate and operatic.

buyer_appeal.lane: Premium streaming / specialty theatrical elevated genre
buyer_appeal.detail: The movie can be packaged around one strong male lead and one equally strong antagonist, with the supporting cast doing the rest of the lifting; that keeps attachment pressure manageable. The contained Flagstaff footprint, plus the current buyer appetite for elevated horror-thrillers with a clean hook, gives it a realistic path to streamer or festival-to-platform launch.

considerations.area: The final-act rules can be clarified sooner.
considerations.detail: The script’s biggest engine is the identity-swap logic, and the version of the story where the audience gets a slightly earlier, cleaner sense of how Gene’s bargain works would make the last act hit even harder. The opening nightmare, the bar pact, and the set reveal already do the heavy lifting — a next pass could foreground the rulebook just a touch earlier so the emotional turn lands with maximum force.

considerations.area: The middle section repeats the same argument in new clothes.
considerations.detail: Champ’s dissatisfaction, Cheyenne’s grounded response, and Gene’s seductive counterpoint are all strong, and the room for the next pass is in varying the emotional beat so each confrontation reveals something new. One lever would be to let one of the later domestic scenes carry a fresh piece of information or a sharper reversal, so the escalation feels even more inevitable.

considerations.area: The production footprint is still very manageable.
considerations.detail: The story lives mostly in homes, an office, a diner, a theater, and a few LA exteriors, which keeps the project in a practical feature lane. The snow work and the mansion/premiere material are the main scale drivers, but the script is still sized for a contained, actor-driven package rather than a large effects build.

considerations.area: The brand and title references invite a clearance pass.
considerations.detail: Sunset Boulevard, It’s a Wonderful Life, Lego, In-N-Out, Range Rover, and Rolls Royce all appear on the page, so a producer would want a clean rights review before lock. None of them define the premise, which means the story can survive a simplification pass if any reference needs to be swapped.
